ravish.e: From Middle English ravyschen, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French ravis-, present participle stem of ravir (“to seize; to take away hastily”), from Vulgar Latin *rapire, from Latin rapere. See also rape.

d.x: The fortreſſe was raſed and beaten downe to the erthe⸝ whiche had coſt moche the makynge therof: […]

d.g: To completely remove (someone or something), especially from a place, a situation, etc.; also, to remove from existence; to destroy, to obliterate.
d.x: VVithout reſpect of ſex, degree or age. / He raceth all his foes vvith fire and ſvvord.

d.g: To erase (a record, text, etc.), originally by scraping; to rub out, to scratch out.
d.x: Suppleyng to Fame, I besought her grace, / And that it wolde please her, full tenderly I prayd, / Owt of her bokis Apollo to rase.

d.g: To wound (someone or part of their body) superficially; to graze.
d.x: [T]he ſvvorde more mercifull then hee to himſelfe, vvith the ſlipping of the pommel, the point ſvvarued, and razed him but vpon the ſide: […]
